extracted.intended_audience: young authors, poets, and literary critics (writers seeking guidance on style, diction, and reception)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, revising, and anticipating the public reception of poems and dramatic lines, with rules about diction, imagery, narrative causation, and how critics/audiences respond. Emphasises stylistic economy, adaptation to medium, and realistic expectations about reviews and recitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of Cause and Effect (narrative causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of Before and After becomes both intelligible and intellectual when we contemplate the succession in the relations of Cause and Effect; confusion is painful. (Passage: 'The sense of Before and After becomes both intelligible and intellectual when, and only when, we contemplate the succession in the relations of Cause and Effect...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative and poetic presentation, ensure antecedents justify consequences so the reader perceives a proportion between past and present events. An intelligible causal ordering gives emotional consolation and a perception of reality; lack of apparent relation between fault and punishment produces a dull, lingering suffering in the reader. Aim for clarity of causal relations rather than leaving events as baffling coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make emotions intelligible by giving them distinguishable forms ('opening out our griefs')
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a healing influence in 'Light and distinct Beholding' that leads the afflicted to communicate their sorrows; 'opening out our griefs' presents them in distinguishable forms instead of an enormous shapeless mist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting grief or strong feeling, render specifics and concrete particulars rather than vague, formless anguish. Turning amorphous sorrow into distinct scenes, images, or complaints reduces its overwhelming size and makes it communicable and alleviating (illustrated by the quotation from Casimir).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust expectations of public reception (subtract panegyric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must subtract to a large amount from the panegyric which may have encouraged them to publish; allowances must be made for private enmity, for the necessity of abuse/ridicule in reviews to sell, and for excitement caused by recital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume private praise equals public acceptance. Anticipate: 1) anonymous or personal enmity that will color reviews, 2) reviewers or periodicals including necessary abuse to sell copies, and 3) inflated reception when poems are recited by celebrated admirers. Plan publishing and reputation management accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for influence of delivery/recitation on reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The enkindling reciter, by perpetual comment of looks and tones, lends his own will and apprehensive faculty to his auditors; they live within the dilated sphere of his intellectual being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem's effect in performance can differ greatly from its effect in print. Authors should be aware that reciters (especially eminent ones) can create a temporary sympathy and excitement not intrinsic to the text. When judging a poem's strength, separate effects due to charismatic delivery from effects due to the written poem itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of reputational pigeonholing affecting critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever appeared with my name was condemned beforehand, as predestined metaphysics... my character as a writer could not easily be more injured by an overt act than it was already in consequence of the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that prior reputation (e.g., being labeled 'metaphysical') predisposes critics and audiences. Writers should expect some criticism to be biased by labels and not purely by the work’s merits; factor this into decisions about when and how to publish controversial or unconventional material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double epithets: restrictive rule for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for the admission of double epithets seems to be this: either that they should be already denizens of our language, such as blood-stained, terror-stricken, self-applauding: or when a new epithet, or one found in books only, is hazarded, that it, at least, be one word, not two words made one by mere virtue of the printers hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use compound epithets sparingly. Prefer established compounds; if coining an epithet from rarer words, fashion it as a single fused word rather than a hyphenated pair. Because English lacks cases and is unfitted for loose compounds, rephrase if a compound is awkward—seek a better word rather than routinely compounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless complexity; prefer simple native expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is translatable in other and simpler words of the same language, without loss of sense or dignity, is bad. N.B.--By dignity I mean the absence of ludicrous and debasing associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an idea can be expressed in simpler, idiomatic English without losing sense or literary dignity, prefer the simpler phrasing. Avoid exotic, bookish, or inflated diction that could be rendered plainly; keep language free from ludicrous or debasing associations introduced by over-elaborate phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine ends before applying rules (rules are means to an end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics are too apt to forget, that rules are but means to an end; consequently, where the ends are different, the rules must be likewise so. We must have ascertained what the end is, before we can determine what the rules ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging a work, first establish the intended purpose and effect. Do not apply prescriptive rules blindly; tailor technical choices (meter, diction, form) to the end you seek. Different genres, audiences, and aims require different rule-sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge collective meaning rather than isolated admired phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of enlightened and highly educated persons ... acknowledged--that they might in all probability have read the same passage again twenty times with undiminished admiration, and without once reflecting, that ... the sense or the diction be the more absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let admiration for individual lines, images, or phrases override assessment of the whole passage's coherence. Editors and readers should test whether the aggregate meaning and logical sense hold together, rather than being seduced by striking isolated turns of phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration/bombast that destroys the visual likeness of similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more simple as a description, or more accurate as a simile... Now here -- the Dog Star, so called, is turned into a real dog, a very odd dog, a fire, fever, plague, and death-breathing, red, air-tainting dog: and the whole visual likeness is lost, while the likeness in the effects is rendered absurd by the exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep similes and images consistent in their domains (visual, affective, causal). Don't expand a simple visual likeness into absurd accumulations of unrelated effects. Excessive amplification (bombast) risks turning a lucid image into nonsense; preserve the original likeness and avoid overblown metaphorical extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the balanced components of 'genius' in critical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the profound sensibility, which is doubtless one of the components of genius, were alone considered, single and unbalanced, it might be fairly described as exposing the individual to a greater chance of mental derangement; but then a more than usual rapidity of association... is a component equally essential; and to the due modification of each by the other the genius itself consists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a writer's gifts, assess the balance of sensibility and associative facility (and other traits), not single qualities in isolation. A strong sensibility without control may be self-destructive; genius often requires the harmonious interplay of multiple faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt lines to the medium and audience (stage suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first [passage]... was spoken in answer to a usurper... In a dramatic poem, which had been submitted... the following passage: 'O we are querulous creatures!...' Aye, here now! (exclaimed the critic) here come Coleridge’s metaphysics! ... the lines were metaphysics [and thus rejected].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure dramatic lines suit theatrical demands (audibility, immediacy, dramatic function). Be mindful that some passages that read well as poetry may be judged unsuitable for the stage for reasons (pace, abstraction) unrelated to their poetic merit. When writing for performance, prioritize clarity, character-appropriateness, and dramatic effect.
